Rules:

- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own

- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.

I'm considering a VBAC with my current pregnancy. My doctor has cautiously told me that it's an option. Can you tell me the benefits of this? I would also like to know the risks involved and the success rate. What are the criteria to work towards making this a successful option?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	What is a VBAC in pregnancy?
     2	 A vaginal birth after cesarean or VBAC is when you give birth through your vagina after previously
     3	having a C-section (cesarean section) delivery. A C-section involves your pregnancy care provider
     4	making a surgical cut (incision) through your belly and uterus to deliver your baby.
     5	
     6	
     7	 The goal of a VBAC is to give a person who had a C-section the chance to have a vaginal delivery
     8	for their next pregnancy. It can sometimes be unsafe to have a vaginal delivery after having one or
     9	more C-section deliveries.
    10	
    11	
    12	 The decision on whether to attempt a VBAC involves considering factors like:
    13	
    14	
    15	 The type of incision your surgeon used for your C-section(s) and if you have had more than one
    16	C-section.
    17	 Your health history.
    18	 If you have any medical conditions.
    19	 The position of the fetus and if the fetus has any known medical conditions.
    20	 Your pregnancy care provider will tell you if they believe a VBAC is safe to try. They can discuss
    21	potential risks and benefits with you. Then, you can choose if you’d like to pursue a VBAC or have
    22	another C-section based on your discussions.
    23	
    24	
    25	 Studies show that up to 75% of people who had one C-section went on to have a successful vaginal
    26	birth in their next pregnancy. But your chance of having a successful VBAC drops to about 50% if
    27	you’ve had two or more prior C-section deliveries.
    28	
    29	
    30	 Healthcare providers sometimes refer to a VBAC as a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC). A TOLAC
    31	is an attempt to have a VBAC. If a TOLAC is successful, the result is a VBAC. If it’s not
    32	successful, the result is another C-section delivery.
    33	
    34	
    35	 Why do people prefer a VBAC instead of another C-section?
    36	 It’s mostly a personal preference. Some people prefer a vaginal delivery, but for some reason, they
    37	haven’t been able to have one. Or a person might prefer a vaginal delivery because recovering from a
    38	C-section typically takes longer.
    39	
    40	
    41	 Even if you want a vaginal delivery, your healthcare provider may recommend another C-section due
    42	to the risks of a VBAC. Or they may tell you it’s OK to try for a VBAC.
    43	
    44	
    45	
    46	
    47	 The benefits of VBAC compared to a C-section include:
    48	
    49	
    50	 Faster recovery and shorter hospital stay.
    51	 No abdominal surgery.
    52	 Avoiding or lowering C-section risks like heavy bleeding and infection.
    53	 Vaginal birth helps clear amniotic fluid from your baby’s lungs as it passes through the birth
    54	canal. This better prepares your baby to breathe oxygen after birth.
    55	 Your baby gets an immune system boost as it travels through the birth canal during a vaginal
    56	delivery.
    57	 Less risk of complications from repeat surgeries like scarring or injuries to nearby organs.
    58	 Personal preference. Some people want the experience of a vaginal birth.
    59	 What are the risks of a VBAC?
    60	 Because a C-section leaves a scar on your uterus, the pressure of labor could cause your uterus to
    61	open (rupture) along your C-section scar. But recent studies show it’s possible to have a safe VBAC
    62	after having a C-section in most cases.
    63	
    64	
    65	 Although rare, a uterine rupture is a serious complication that can have life-threatening results.
    66	If you’re at a high risk for uterine rupture, your healthcare provider will typically not attempt a
    67	VBAC.
    68	
    69	
    70	 Other risks of attempting a VBAC are:
    71	
    72	
    73	 Blood loss.
    74	 Infection.
    75	 Emergency C-section (which is riskier than a planned C-section).
    76	 What’s the risk of a uterine rupture if you’ve had a previous C-section?
    77	 The risk of uterine rupture if you’ve had a C-section with a transverse cut (sideways across the
    78	lower part of the uterus) is about 0.9% or slightly less than 1 in 100.
    79	
    80	
    81	 Does the type of incision I got from my last C-section matter if I want a VBAC?
    82	 Yes. There are different types of C-section incisions:
    83	
    84	
    85	 A low transverse incision has the lowest risk of uterine rupture. This horizontal cut is made
    86	across the lower, thinner part of your uterus.
    87	 A low vertical incision (up and down cut) has a higher risk of rupture than a low transverse
    88	incision. This vertical cut is made in the lower, thinner part of your uterus.
    89	 A high vertical incision (“classical” incision) in the upper part of your uterus has the highest
    90	risk of uterine rupture. Surgeons may need to use this type of incision for a premature baby or one
    91	that’s in a difficult position to deliver.
    92	 The location and direction of the outer incision on your belly doesn’t mean that the incision in
    93	your uterus is in the same location or the same direction. For example, it may appear that the scar
    94	on your belly is transverse, yet the scar on your uterus is vertical.
    95	
    96	
    97	 The information about the location and direction of the incision on your uterus should be in your
    98	medical records. When you talk about how safe VBAC is with your provider, make sure they look at
    99	your medical records and the reasons for any C-sections you’ve had.
   100	
   101	
   102	 Is a VBAC safer than a repeat C-section?
   103	 Talk with your healthcare provider about your health history, current pregnancy and why you had a
   104	C-section in your last pregnancy.
   105	
   106	
   107	 Your chances of having a successful VBAC may be higher if you:
   108	
   109	
   110	 Have had previous C-section deliveries (one or two) with low transverse incisions.
   111	 Have had a vaginal birth before.
   112	 Haven’t had any other uterine surgeries (such as fibroid removal, also called myomectomy).
   113	 Have no history of uterine rupture.
   114	 Don’t have a medical condition (like fibroids or problems with the location of your placenta) that
   115	makes a vaginal delivery risky.
   116	 Go into labor on your own before your due date.
   117	 If you’ve already had a successful VBAC — without complications such as ruptured uterus — you’re
   118	more likely to have successful future vaginal deliveries.
   119	
   120	
   121	 Your chances of having a successful VBAC may be lower if you:
   122	
   123	
   124	 Had a prior C-section due to labor not progressing. This means you didn’t dilate (cervix opens) or
   125	efface (cervix shortens) during a vaginal delivery.
   126	 Are older than 35.
   127	 Have obesity or overweight.
   128	 Are giving birth to a large fetus or expecting multiples.
   129	 Are past your due date.
   130	 Had a baby within the last 18 months (short time between pregnancies).
   131	 Have preeclampsia. (Healthcare providers may prefer a C-section delivery.)
   132	 What are the risks of multiple C-sections?
   133	 There isn’t a set number of C-sections you can have. But some evidence shows that people who have
   134	many C-sections are at a higher risk for:
   135	
   136	
   137	 Heavy bleeding.
   138	 Bladder and bowel injury.
   139	 Infection.
   140	 Placental conditions like placenta previa or placenta accreta in a future pregnancy where the
   141	placenta is abnormally attached.
   142	 Uterine rupture.
   143	 Adhesions (scarring).
   144	 These risks vary and depend mostly on your health history and the specific circumstances of each
   145	pregnancy and delivery. Your healthcare provider is the best person to talk to about the risks and
   146	benefits of a repeat C-section versus a VBAC.
   147	
   148	
   149	
   150	
   151	 Topics to discuss with your pregnancy care provider include:
   152	
   153	
   154	 Past pregnancies and deliveries.

The main risk is uterine rupture: "Because a C-section leaves a scar on your uterus, the pressure of labor could cause your uterus to open (rupture) along your C-section scar." The specific risk is: "The risk of uterine rupture if you've had a C-section with a transverse cut (sideways across the lower part of the uterus) is about 0.9% or slightly less than 1 in 100."

- "Infection."
- "Emergency C-section (which is riskier than a planned C-section)."

## Success rate

- "Don't have a medical condition (like fibroids or problems with the location of your placenta) that makes a vaginal delivery risky."

- "Are older than 35."
- "Have obesity or overweight."
- "Are giving birth to a large fetus or expecting multiples."
- "Are past your due date."
- "Had a baby within the last 18 months (short time between pregnancies)."
- "Have preeclampsia. (Healthcare providers may prefer a C-section delivery.)"

The document also emphasizes that the type of incision matters: "A low transverse incision has the lowest risk of uterine rupture," while a low vertical incision has higher risk and a high vertical ("classical") incision has the highest risk. It recommends that "When you talk about how safe VBAC is with your provider, make sure they look at your medical records and the reasons for any C-sections you've had."

Suggested topics to discuss with your provider include: "Past pregnancies and deliveries," "Reason(s) you had a C-section," "Safety of VBAC and a repeat C-section for you and your baby," "A plan for inducing labor (or not)," and "If the healthcare facility can manage emergency deliveries."

## Benefits of VBAC compared to a C-section

The document lists the following benefits:
- "Faster recovery and shorter hospital stay." (doc.txt)
- "No abdominal surgery." (doc.txt)
- "Avoiding or lowering C-section risks like heavy bleeding and infection." (doc.txt)
- "Vaginal birth helps clear amniotic fluid from your baby's lungs as it passes through the birth canal. This better prepares your baby to breathe oxygen after birth." (doc.txt)
- "Your baby gets an immune system boost as it travels through the birth canal during a vaginal delivery." (doc.txt)
- "Less risk of complications from repeat surgeries like scarring or injuries to nearby organs." (doc.txt)
- "Personal preference. Some people want the experience of a vaginal birth." (doc.txt)

## Risks of VBAC

The main risk is uterine rupture: "Because a C-section leaves a scar on your uterus, the pressure of labor could cause your uterus to open (rupture) along your C-section scar." (doc.txt) The document notes that "Although rare, a uterine rupture is a serious complication that can have life-threatening results." (doc.txt) The specific risk is: "The risk of uterine rupture if you've had a C-section with a transverse cut (sideways across the lower part of the uterus) is about 0.9% or slightly less than 1 in 100." (doc.txt)

Other risks of attempting a VBAC are:
- "Blood loss." (doc.txt)
- "Infection." (doc.txt)
- "Emergency C-section (which is riskier than a planned C-section)." (doc.txt)

The document also notes that "it's possible to have a safe VBAC after having a C-section in most cases" (doc.txt), and that if you're at high risk for uterine rupture, "your healthcare provider will typically not attempt a VBAC." (doc.txt)

## Success rate

"Studies show that up to 75% of people who had one C-section went on to have a successful vaginal birth in their next pregnancy. But your chance of having a successful VBAC drops to about 50% if you've had two or more prior C-section deliveries." (doc.txt)

## Criteria that favor a successful VBAC

Your chances may be **higher** if you:
- "Have had previous C-section deliveries (one or two) with low transverse incisions." (doc.txt)
- "Have had a vaginal birth before." (doc.txt)
- "Haven't had any other uterine surgeries (such as fibroid removal, also called myomectomy)." (doc.txt)
- "Have no history of uterine rupture." (doc.txt)
- "Don't have a medical condition (like fibroids or problems with the location of your placenta) that makes a vaginal delivery risky." (doc.txt)
- "Go into labor on your own before your due date." (doc.txt)
- If you've "already had a successful VBAC — without complications such as ruptured uterus — you're more likely to have successful future vaginal deliveries." (doc.txt)

Your chances may be **lower** if you:
- "Had a prior C-section due to labor not progressing." (doc.txt)

- "Have obesity or overweight." (doc.txt)
- "Are giving birth to a large fetus or expecting multiples." (doc.txt)
- "Are past your due date." (doc.txt)
- "Had a baby within the last 18 months (short time between pregnancies)." (doc.txt)
- "Have preeclampsia. (Healthcare providers may prefer a C-section delivery.)" (doc.txt)

The document also emphasizes that the type of incision matters: "A low transverse incision has the lowest risk of uterine rupture" (doc.txt), while a low vertical incision has higher risk and a high vertical ("classical") incision has the highest risk. ## Benefits of VBAC compared to a C-section

- "Faster recovery and shorter hospital stay." (doc.txt)

- "Blood loss." (doc.txt)
- "Infection." (doc.txt)
- "Emergency C-section (which is riskier than a planned C-section)." (doc.txt)

## Success rate

"Studies show that up to 75% of people who had one C-section went on to have a successful vaginal birth in their next pregnancy. But your chance of having a successful VBAC drops to about 50% if you've had two or more prior C-section deliveries." (doc.txt)

- "Have had a vaginal birth before." (doc.txt)

- "Are giving birth to a large fetus or expecting multiples." (doc.txt)
- "Are past your due date." (doc.txt)
- "Had a baby within the last 18 months (short time between pregnancies)." (doc.txt)
